steps.text: Write the History section of an encyclopedia article on algorithmically random sequences, covering von Mises's idea of a collective and why it was replaced by Martin-Löf's definition.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
### Richard von Mises
- Collectives and admissible rules
  - von Mises formalized "test for randomness"; random = passes all tests
  - "collective" (kollektiv): infinite binary string x_{1:\infty} with
    - limit \lim_n \frac 1n \sum_{i=1}^n x_i = p \in (0, 1)
    - any "admissible" rule picking infinite subsequence (x_{m_i})_i still gives \lim_n \frac 1n \sum_{i=1}^n x_{m_i} = p
  - principle called "impossibility of a gambling system"
  - picking a subsequence: binary function \phi on x_{1:k}, outputs 0 or 1; 1 -> add x_{k+1}
  - some rules abstain forever on some sequences; only consider ones that pick an infinite subsequence
- Gambling interpretation
  - each infinite binary string = coin-flip game; admissible rule = when a gambler bets
  - collective = no gambler does better than another in the long run; no gambling system works
- Generalization
  - binary -> countable alphabet: each letter's frequency converges to a limit > 0; same limit in any admissible subsequence
  - usually: rules computable by a Turing machine, p=1/2 -> Mises–Wald–Church random sequences
  - not a restriction: from p=1/2 can construct any other computable p \in (0, 1)
  - "Church" = Alonzo Church, 1940 paper, Turing-computable rules
- Ville's objection
  - definition not strong enough
  - intuition: long-time average should oscillate on both sides of p (like random walk crossing origin infinitely often)
  - Jean Ville: even with countably many rules, binary sequence tending to p fraction of ones, but every finite prefix has fraction < p
### Per Martin-Löf
- Problem
  - Ville construction -> Mises–Wald–Church not good enough; fails some laws of randomness
  - e.g. a law of the iterated logarithm: \limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{-\sum_{k=1}^n (x_k - 1/2)}{\sqrt{2n \log\log n}} \neq 1
  - naive fix: satisfy all laws of randomness (property holding with probability 1)
  - but for each y_{1:\infty} \in 2^\N, x_{1:\infty} \neq y_{1:\infty} is such a law -> no random sequences
- Martin-Löf randomness (1966)
  - only Turing-computable laws of randomness
  - random iff passes all Turing-computable tests
- Thesis
  - Martin-Löf–Chaitin Thesis: definition "correctly" captures intuitive randomness
  - somewhat similar to the Church–Turing thesis

steps.text:
### Richard von Mises

Richard von Mises formalized the idea of a test for randomness, so that a random sequence could be defined as a sequence that passed all the tests for randomness. He defined a "collective" (kollektiv) as an infinite binary string x_{1:\infty} with these properties:

There is a limit \lim_n \frac 1n \sum_{i=1}^n x_i = p \in (0, 1) .

For any "admissible" rule that picks out an infinite subsequence (x_{m_i})_i from the string, we still get \lim_n \frac 1n \sum_{i=1}^n x_{m_i} = p . He called this principle the "impossibility of a gambling system".

To pick out a subsequence, you first pick a binary function \phi , which takes any binary string x_{1:k} and outputs 0 or 1. If the output is 1, x_{k+1} is added to the subsequence, otherwise we go on. With this definition some admissible rules might abstain forever on some sequences, and so they never pick out an infinite subsequence. We only consider the rules that do pick an infinite subsequence.

Another way to say this is that each infinite binary string is a coin-flip game, and an admissible rule is a way for a gambler to decide when to bet. A collective is then a coin-flip game where no gambler can do better than another gambler over the long run. So there is no gambling system that works for the game.

- Generalization
  - binary -> countable alphabet: frequency of each letter converges to a limit greater than zero; same limit in any admissible subsequence (x_{m_i})_i
  - usually rules computable by a Turing machine, p=1/2 -> Mises–Wald–Church random sequences
  - not a restriction: from p=1/2 can construct any other computable p \in (0, 1)
  - "Church" = Alonzo Church, 1940 paper proposing Turing-computable rules
- Ville's objection
  - definition not strong enough
  - long-time average should oscillate on both sides of p , like random walk crossing origin infinitely many times
  - Jean Ville: even with countably many rules, a binary sequence tends to p fraction of ones but every finite prefix has fraction less than p
### Per Martin-Löf
- Ville construction -> Mises–Wald–Church not good enough; fails a law of the iterated logarithm: \limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{-\sum_{k=1}^n (x_k - 1/2)}{\sqrt{2n \log\log n}} \neq 1
- naive fix (all laws of randomness, i.e. probability 1 properties) fails: x_{1:\infty} \neq y_{1:\infty} for each y_{1:\infty} \in 2^\N -> no random sequences
- Martin-Löf (1966): only Turing-computable laws; random iff passes all Turing-computable tests
- Martin-Löf–Chaitin Thesis: "correctly" captures intuitive randomness; somewhat similar to Church–Turing thesis

steps.text:
### Richard von Mises

Richard von Mises formalized the idea of a test for randomness, so that a random sequence could be defined as a sequence that passed all the tests for randomness. He defined a "collective" (kollektiv) as an infinite binary string x_{1:\infty} with these properties:

There is a limit \lim_n \frac 1n \sum_{i=1}^n x_i = p \in (0, 1) .

For any "admissible" rule that picks out an infinite subsequence (x_{m_i})_i from the string, we still get \lim_n \frac 1n \sum_{i=1}^n x_{m_i} = p . He called this principle the "impossibility of a gambling system".

To pick out a subsequence, you first pick a binary function \phi , which takes any binary string x_{1:k} and outputs 0 or 1. If the output is 1, x_{k+1} is added to the subsequence, otherwise we go on. With this definition some admissible rules might abstain forever on some sequences, and so they never pick out an infinite subsequence. We only consider the rules that do pick an infinite subsequence.

Another way to say this is that each infinite binary string is a coin-flip game, and an admissible rule is a way for a gambler to decide when to bet. A collective is then a coin-flip game where no gambler can do better than another gambler over the long run. So there is no gambling system that works for the game.

The definition can be generalized from a binary alphabet to a countable alphabet:

The frequency of each letter converges to a limit that is greater than zero.

For any "admissible" rule that picks out an infinite subsequence (x_{m_i})_i from the string, the frequency of each letter in the subsequence still converges to the same limit.

Usually the admissible rules are defined as rules computable by a Turing machine, and p=1/2 is required. This gives the Mises–Wald–Church random sequences. This is not really a restriction, because from a sequence with p=1/2 we can construct random sequences with any other computable p \in (0, 1) . ("Church" here is Alonzo Church, who proposed using Turing-computable rules in a 1940 paper.)

However, it turned out that this definition was not strong enough.

Intuitively, the long-time average of a random sequence should oscillate on both sides of p , in the same way that a random walk should cross the origin infinitely many times. But Jean Ville showed that, even with countably many rules, there is a binary sequence that tends towards p fraction of ones, but where the fraction of ones is less than p for every finite prefix.

### Per Martin-Löf

The Ville construction suggests that randomness in the Mises–Wald–Church sense is not good enough, because some random sequences do not satisfy some laws of randomness. For example, the Ville construction does not satisfy one of the laws of the iterated logarithm: \limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{-\sum_{k=1}^n (x_k - 1/2)}{\sqrt{2n \log\log n}} \neq 1 The naive way to fix this is to require a sequence to satisfy all possible laws of randomness, where a "law of randomness" is a property that all sequences satisfy with probability 1. But then for each infinite sequence y_{1:\infty} \in 2^\N , there is a law of randomness that x_{1:\infty} \neq y_{1:\infty} , and so we get the conclusion that there are no random sequences at all.

Per Martin-Löf (1966) defined "Martin-Löf randomness" by allowing only laws of randomness that are Turing-computable. So a sequence is random iff it passes all the Turing-computable tests of randomness.

The thesis that the definition of Martin-Löf randomness "correctly" captures the intuitive idea of randomness has been called the Martin-Löf–Chaitin Thesis. It is somewhat similar to the Church–Turing thesis.

steps.text:
### Richard von Mises

Richard von Mises formalized the notion of a test for randomness in order to define a random sequence as one that passed all tests for randomness. He defined a "collective" (kollektiv) to be an infinite binary string x_{1:\infty} such that

There exists a limit \lim_n \frac 1n \sum_{i=1}^n x_i = p \in (0, 1) .

For any "admissible" rule that picks out an infinite subsequence (x_{m_i})_i from the string, we still have \lim_n \frac 1n \sum_{i=1}^n x_{m_i} = p . He called this principle the "impossibility of a gambling system".

To pick out a subsequence, first pick a binary function \phi that, given any binary string x_{1:k} , outputs either 0 or 1. If it outputs 1, we add x_{k+1} to the subsequence; otherwise we continue. Under this definition, some admissible rules might abstain forever on some sequences and so fail to pick out an infinite subsequence. We only consider those that do pick an infinite subsequence.

Put another way, each infinite binary string is a coin-flip game, and an admissible rule is a way for a gambler to decide when to place bets. A collective is a coin-flip game in which no gambler can do better than another over the long run; that is, no gambling system works for the game.

The definition generalizes from a binary alphabet to a countable alphabet:

The frequency of each letter converges to a limit greater than zero.

For any "admissible" rule that picks out an infinite subsequence (x_{m_i})_i from the string, the frequency of each letter in the subsequence still converges to the same limit.

Usually the admissible rules are defined to be rules computable by a Turing machine, and we require p=1/2 . This gives the Mises–Wald–Church random sequences. This is not a restriction, since given a sequence with p=1/2 , we can construct random sequences with any other computable p \in (0, 1) .[1] (Here "Church" refers to Alonzo Church, whose 1940 paper proposed using Turing-computable rules.[2])

However, this definition turned out not to be strong enough.

Intuitively, the long-time average of a random sequence should oscillate on both sides of p , just as a random walk should cross the origin infinitely many times. However, Jean Ville showed that, even with countably many rules, there is a binary sequence that tends towards p fraction of ones but whose fraction of ones is less than p for every finite prefix.[3]

### Per Martin-Löf

The Ville construction suggests that the Mises–Wald–Church sense of randomness is not good enough, since some random sequences fail some laws of randomness. For example, the Ville construction does not satisfy one of the laws of the iterated logarithm: \limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{-\sum_{k=1}^n (x_k - 1/2)}{\sqrt{2n \log\log n}} \neq 1 Naively, one could fix this by requiring a sequence to satisfy all possible laws of randomness, where a "law of randomness" is a property satisfied by all sequences with probability 1. However, for each infinite sequence y_{1:\infty} \in 2^\N , there is a law of randomness that x_{1:\infty} \neq y_{1:\infty} , which leads to the conclusion that there are no random sequences.

Per Martin-Löf (1966)[4] defined "Martin-Löf randomness" by allowing only laws of randomness that are Turing-computable. In other words, a sequence is random iff it passes all Turing-computable tests of randomness.

The thesis that the definition of Martin-Löf randomness "correctly" captures the intuitive notion of randomness has been called the Martin-Löf–Chaitin Thesis; it is somewhat similar to the Church–Turing thesis.[5]

References:
[1] Li, Ming. (2019). An introduction to Kolmogorov complexity and its applications. Springer.
[2] Copeland, Arthur H.. (June 1940). Alonzo Church. On the concept of a random sequence. Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society, vol. 46 (1940), pp. 130–135.. The Journal of Symbolic Logic. doi:10.2307/2266178
[3] Ville, J. (1939). Étude critique de la notion de collectif, Monographies des Probabilités, Calcul des Probabilités et ses Applications, Gauthier-Villars.
[4] Martin-Löf, Per. (1966-12-01). The definition of random sequences. Information and Control. doi:10.1016/S0019-9958(66)80018-9
[5] Jean-Paul Delahaye, Randomness, Unpredictability and Absence of Order, in Philosophy of Probability, p. 145–167, Springer 1993.
